content: Blastocystis hominis Blastocystis hominis is a protozoan parasite that has been revisited in research due to its potential role in human gastrointestinal diseases. Studies have identified viable cysts of this organism in sewage samples from Scotland and Malaysia, highlighting its environmental presence. Recent advancements in research have focused on understanding its pathogenicity and epidemiology, though much remains unknown. Cryptosporidium Cryptosporidium is an intracellular coccidian parasite with a complex life cycle involving both sexual and asexual reproduction. Its thick-walled oocysts, measuring 4–6 µm in diameter, are excreted in feces and are highly resistant to environmental conditions. Human infections are primarily caused by Cryptosporidium hominis and the cattle genotype of Cryptosporidium parvum, though other species can occasionally infect humans. Discovered as a human pathogen in 1976, it was first linked to waterborne transmission in 1984. Cryptosporidiosis typically causes self-limiting diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, and fever in healthy individuals, but it can be life-threatening in immunocompromised patients. Outbreaks, such as the 1993 Milwaukee incident infecting over 400,000 people, underscore its public health significance. Transmission occurs via the fecal-oral route, contaminated water, food, and direct contact with infected animals or humans. Oocysts are highly infectious, with fewer than 10 oocysts capable of causing infection. They are resistant to chlorine disinfection but can be inactivated by UV light. Effective water treatment and source protection are critical for managing risks. Cyclospora cayetanensis Cyclospora cayetanensis is a single-celled coccidian parasite that produces thick-walled oocysts measuring 8–10 µm in diameter. These oocysts are excreted in feces and require 7–12 days in the environment to sporulate and become infectious. Cyclospora is an emerging waterborne pathogen, causing cyclosporiasis, which manifests as watery diarrhea, abdominal cramps, weight loss, anorexia, and sometimes fever or vomiting. Relapsing illness is common. Humans are the only known host, and transmission occurs through contaminated water or food, often linked to crops irrigated with contaminated water. Drinking water has been implicated in outbreaks, such as one in Chicago in 1990 and another in Nepal among soldiers. Oocysts are resistant to chlorination, and prevention focuses on source water protection and adequate treatment. Entamoeba histolytica Entamoeba histolytica is the most prevalent intestinal protozoan pathogen worldwide. It exists as a feeding trophozoite (10–60 µm) and a dormant cyst (10–20 µm). Infection occurs through ingestion of cysts, often via contaminated water or food. Most infections (85–95%) are asymptomatic, but acute intestinal amoebiasis can cause dysentery, colitis, and characteristic flask-shaped ulcers in the gastrointestinal tract. In severe cases, the parasite can invade other organs, such as the liver, lungs, or brain, with potentially fatal outcomes. Humans are the primary reservoir, and transmission occurs through person-to-person contact, contaminated water, or food. Sexual transmission has also been documented. Giardia intestinalis Giardia intestinalis (also known as G. lamblia or G. duodenalis) is a flagellated protozoan that infects the gastrointestinal tract of humans and animals. Its life cycle includes a flagellated trophozoite and an infectious cyst, which is excreted in large numbers in feces. Symptoms of giardiasis include diarrhea, abdominal cramps, and, in severe cases, malabsorption, particularly in young children. Infections can be asymptomatic, with up to 20% of children in daycare centers excreting cysts without symptoms. Giardia cysts are robust, surviving for weeks to months in freshwater, and are resistant to chlorine disinfection. Transmission occurs through person-to-person contact, contaminated water, and food. Waterborne outbreaks have been documented for over 30 years, making Giardia a significant concern in drinking water safety. Isospora belli Isospora belli is a coccidian parasite that infects humans, its only known host. It undergoes sexual reproduction in the human intestine, and unsporulated oocysts are excreted in feces. Sporulation occurs in the environment within 1–2 days, producing infectious oocysts. Isosporiasis causes symptoms similar to cryptosporidiosis and giardiasis, including diarrhea, abdominal pain, and weight loss. Infections are often self-limiting but can persist for months in immunocompromised individuals, leading to malabsorption and chronic symptoms. Transmission is associated with poor sanitation and contaminated food or water, though waterborne transmission has not been confirmed. Oocysts are resistant to disinfection but may be removed by filtration. Microsporidia Microsporidia are obligate intracellular parasites, initially classified as protozoa but now considered fungi. They are among the smallest eukaryotes, with spores measuring 1–5 µm. Infection occurs when spores inject their sporoplasm into host cells, initiating replication. Microsporidia infect a wide range of animals, including humans, and are emerging pathogens, particularly in immunocompromised individuals such as those with AIDS. Clinical manifestations include chronic diarrhea, dehydration, and weight loss, with prolonged illness reported in some cases. Spores are excreted in feces, urine, and respiratory secretions, and their presence in water sources has been documented. They are resistant to environmental conditions and may survive for months in water. Further research is needed to understand their transmission and prevalence in water environments.
